  target-python-version = "3.14"
  use-title-as-name = true

The counts, presets and options come from your schema and the installed version. The report has these sections:

Section Meaning Schema The signals the rules read: components, inline objects and enums, shared property names, repeated shapes, titles, unions and their tags, key style, constraint keywords (uniqueItems; patternProperties, with how many a typed map cannot express; multipleOf; nullable in OpenAPI 3.0 and AsyncAPI 2 documents; boolean exclusive bounds), the formats generation maps to a type (int32/int64 ranges are not enforced), and the integer, number and boolean schemas. Start from The latest dated standard preset for your output model type and target Python version, and the rules it already satisfies. It is the practical preset only when you configured a practical preset, or when no option can set a value a rule needs on the standard preset (the notes then say which). Add Options to add on top of the preset. Each names its rule in brackets, the reason, caveat: lines for known limits, measured: lines with the effect seen on public schemas, and a trial: line with the candidates without and with it, their class and problem-name counts, and up to three class names it changes in your schema. Left out after the trial Options the rules recommend that the selected candidate does without, because your schema's class names score better without them. Consider Options the schema has signals for and against (against:). Decide from your schema; they are in the command only when the candidate with them scores best. Optional (validation) Options for checks the schema declares that the models leave out by default, such as --generate-schema-validators for uniqueItems and for patternProperties a typed map cannot express (beside declared properties, with several patterns, or with other keys allowed) with Pydantic v2 models. They are experimental or change runtime behaviour, so they are not in the command; validate sample data with the generated models first. Optional (policy) Options that depend on what input your project accepts rather than on the schema, such as --strict-types, which rejects the strings and booleans Pydantic's lax mode coerces into numbers and booleans. They are never in the command. Not recommended Options a rule argues against for this schema. Trial The compared candidates with their class counts, problem names, median name length, and unconstrained: the fields dcg warns it generates without some of their constraints, counted per module in the generation each candidate keeps; selected marks the recommended one. Changes from the current configuration The class names the recommended configuration changes from the configuration you run now, matched by the internal identity paths of their models. Your configuration Options you set that differ from the rules, and a newer preset when you set an older one. Your values are kept. Notes Assumptions, such as the target Python version used when you did not set one. Command / pyproject.toml The same recommendation as a command and as configuration.

items.title: Apply it
items.text:
• No pyproject.toml configuration yet: copy the pyproject.toml block into your pyproject.toml, add output, and run datamodel-codegen. Or run the printed command with --output.
  • Existing [tool.datamodel-codegen] table: the report shows pyproject.toml: keys to add or change with only the keys to add or change. Keys the recommender did not decide are never shown as removed. With --profile or --job, the changes are for that profile or job table.
  • Preset given on the command line: the printed command includes the additions.

Options you set on the command line or in pyproject.toml always stay as you set them. When a rule disagrees, the report lists it under "Your configuration" instead of changing it. Adopting a new naming option can rename generated classes: "Changes from the current configuration" counts them and shows examples, so review imports of the generated models before switching an existing project.

--http-headers and --http-query-parameters are not repeated in the printed command, and URLs are shown without their user information, query, and fragment; add them again when you run it. A remote input is read once, checked against the remote reference lock as generation checks it (--locked, --lockfile), and the lock is never written.

items.title: JSON output
items.text:
For tools and coding agents, add --output-format json:

datamodel-codegen --input openapi.yaml --input-file-type openapi --recommend-options --output-format json
datamodel-codegen --output-format-json-schema recommend-options

The payload has kind: "recommend-options" and contains the mode that ran (full when candidates were compared), the signals, the starting preset under baseline, the recommendations, left_out, consider, not_recommended and disagreements entries (each with its rule, set config values, CLI arguments, and the trial candidates and class-name changes that measured it), the optional validation and policy entries (never in arguments or config), the compared candidates under trial (each with its metrics, its dropped_constraint_warnings, and stability with --diff-against, plus the ranking, the selected label, the migration from the current configuration, and the dropped (candidates beyond the limit) and remeasured counts), notes, the full command as arguments, the config table, and the text report as content. rules_revision identifies the rule data and trial.metrics_version the class-name metrics that produced it.

items.title: Ask an LLM with the recommendation
items.text:
Add --recommend-options to a --generate-prompt command to include the report in the prompt, under "Schema analysis and recommended options", and ask the LLM to start from the recommended command and give a reason for every option it changes. With --output-format json, the prompt payload has the recommendation payload as recommendation.

datamodel-codegen --input openapi.yaml --input-file-type openapi --recommend-options \
  --generate-prompt "Which options keep the class names stable across schema versions?"

items.title: What it measures
items.text:
• It reads the input once and measures the schema signals without generating models: how the schemas are named and nested, and which constraint keywords and formats they use. Keywords beside a $ref count where the document's version applies them (JSON Schema 2019-09 and later, OpenAPI 3.1 and later, AsyncAPI 3).
  • For OpenAPI, it measures what your --openapi-scopes generate: component schemas with the schemas scope (otherwise only those the operations reference), and request, response, parameter, webhook, and request body schemas with those scopes, filtered by --openapi-include-paths; parameter schemas follow every walked operation. For AsyncAPI, it measures component schemas and the payload and header schemas of messages in components and channels, including multi-format schema objects.
  • Generation reads the definitions of a Swagger 2.0 document with --input-file-type jsonschema, so that is how it is analysed. With --input-file-type openapi, generation finds no models in it; the report says so and prints no command or pyproject.toml block.
  • With --generate-server or --generate-client, it checks the target's options and applies the settings the target implies (such as the api scope and Python 3.11) as generation does, so the recommendation starts from a preset the target can use.
  • It applies the rules to the signals and computes the options on top of the latest preset for your output model type and target Python version.
  • Schema rules cover OpenAPI, AsyncAPI, and JSON Schema documents. For other input types, a directory input, or --input-model, it recommends only the preset.
  • When --target-python-version is not set, it assumes the default target and says so in the notes.

It cannot be combined with --check, --watch, --all-jobs, more than one --job, --generate-pyproject-config, --generate-cli-command, --install-skill, --list-deprecations, or --list-experimental.

items.title: How candidates are compared
items.text:
The recommender then generates these configurations of your command in memory, with formatting off, and reads the class names each one gives your schema:

  • current: the configuration as you run it now, without the recommended preset. It is measured for the changes from your configuration and never selected.
  • preset: the latest dated preset with your options.
  • recommended: the preset with the options the rules add.
  • recommended + DECISION: the recommendation with each option the schema also argues against (Consider).
  • recommended - DECISION: the recommendation without each option it adds.

With a preset already configured, your configuration is the starting point and is labelled current. A configuration is generated once under its first label, and at most eight are compared; the last ones are left out first, and the notes say so.

Each candidate's class names are measured like the naming benchmark the rules come from. A name is a problem when it is numbered (Status1), contains a status code, is a generic word (Item, Data), is longer than 40 characters, repeats a word the schema does not repeat (ShapeShape), takes a component's name from the component, or names an inline model like an unrelated component. A name can have several of these problems: a numbered name over 40 characters is both numbered and long. Candidates are ranked by, in order: fewer numbered or doubled names; fewer other problem names, such as names over 40 characters; with --diff-against, fewer classes renamed between the previous and the current schema; a shorter median name; then fewer fields that dcg warns it generates without some of their constraints. Numbered names count as worse than long descriptive names: Event2 says nothing about the class, while a long name still describes it. Only when two candidates generate exactly the same class names does the one with fewer added options rank first; other ties keep the order above. The best candidate other than current is selected, and the command and pyproject.toml block carry its options.

The trial: line of each option compares the candidates without and with it on the selected configuration, so it shows what that one option changes in the recommended command. When the selected candidate is not the rules' recommendation, the trial also generates the selected configuration without or with each option it needs for those lines; these rows are listed last and never selected.

Classes are matched by the internal identity paths of their models, which stay the same across configurations and are never written; the reports call this matching by schema location. The locations in the examples are described from the JSON Pointer that --emit-model-metadata writes as source_ref: the named schema or operation, then each inline step after > (a property reads as its name, a union branch oneOf 0, an array item item).

A candidate whose generation fails is listed as rejected with a one-line reason and never selected. If every candidate fails, the options are the rules' recommendation alone. The candidates share the parsed input and fetch each remote document once; they print nothing, and the notes say which input type the trial read when it was not given. With --generate-server or --generate-client, the trial compares the models only.

Candidates are compared when the schema is estimated at up to 3000 models: its components, inline objects and enums, and inline union variants, plus those of --diff-against. The limit is a model count, never a time, so the same schema always gives the same report. Larger schemas, and inputs whose size cannot be estimated (input types without schema rules, directories, --input-model), get the rules only; the notes give the command that compares the candidates anyway, for every input type.

items.title: Stability between schema versions
items.text:
Pass the previous version of the schema with --diff-against (and --output, which selects the layout as for generation) to also rank candidates by how many classes they rename between the versions:

datamodel-codegen --input openapi.yaml --diff-against openapi.previous.yaml --output models.py --recommend-options

Every candidate is then generated for both versions, and the Trial table gains a renamed column.

items.title: How recommendations are maintained
items.text:
• Rules are data. The rules ship in the package as recommender_rules.json. Each rule maps schema signals to option values and carries its reason, caveats, and evidence. Rule values are validated through the same model as presets, so a rule cannot name an option that does not exist.
  • Every option is registered. Each option has an entry in the rule data: either the rules that decide it or the reason the recommender leaves it to you (input/output paths, the target, runtime behaviour, formatting, and so on). A new option cannot be released without that decision.
  • Calibration. The rules were derived from measurements of class names on public API descriptions and schemas, and rule changes go through normal reviewed pull requests. The report notes when the rules were calibrated on other presets than the one it starts from.
  • Presets stay immutable. A dated preset never changes. An option that the rules recommend for most schemas is proposed for a new dated preset; once it exists, the recommendation starts from it and stops listing that option.

items.title: FAQ
items.text:
Does it generate code? It writes nothing. To compare candidates, it generates their models in memory and reads only the class names.

Does it change my pyproject.toml? No. It prints a command and a configuration block; you decide what to apply.

Will it override options I set? No. Explicit options are kept, and disagreements are reported under "Your configuration".

Is the output stable? The same input, options, and installed version give the same report. The report does not depend on the machine or on installed libraries, and whether candidates are compared depends on the schema size, not on time. Upgrading datamodel-code-generator can change the recommendation when a new preset or a rule revision is released.

Why is an option I expected missing? Either the preset already sets it (listed under "Start from"), the schema does not show the signal its rule needs, the candidate without it scored better on your schema (listed under "Left out after the trial"), it is an optional validation or policy option that stays out of the command (listed under "Optional"), or the option is a project decision the recommender never makes. Check Presets and the CLI Reference for the full list of options.

items.title: 📦 Root Models and Type Aliases
items.text: When a schema defines a simple type (not an object with properties), datamodel-code-generator creates a root model. If you don't want to introduce a new level of attribute access (.root) or want to use generated types as plain Python types in non-Pydantic code, you can use the --use-type-alias flag to generate type aliases instead of root models.

items.title: ⚠️ Notes and Limitations
items.text:
This functionality is experimental! Here are a few known issues:

  • 📌 RootModel and type aliases do not fully support field-specific metadata (default, alias, etc). See Named Type Aliases for details.
  • 🚫 Type aliases do not support some RootModel features (e.g. model_config)
  • 📄 A RootModel or type alias is also generated for the main schema, allowing you to define a single type alias from a schema file (e.g. model.json containing {"title": "MyString", "type": "string"})
  • 🧩 Pydantic v2 type aliases express constraints as Annotated[int, Field(ge=1)] instead of conint(ge=1), because mypy and Pyright reject call expressions in type aliases. A Decimal multipleOf uses annotated_types.MultipleOf, because Field types multiple_of as a float. Validation, serialization, and JSON schema stay the same, except that on Pydantic 2.0.x a string alias with minLength: 0 now keeps minLength: 0 in its JSON schema.
  • 🔤 Pydantic v2 type aliases (--use-type-alias and pydantic_v2.dataclass output) cannot select Python's regex engine through model_config, so patterns that need it, such as lookaround assertions, are generated as compiled re.compile(...) patterns. These aliases require Pydantic 2.8 or later in the environment that runs the generated code, because Pydantic 2.8 added support for compiled patterns. With --target-pydantic-version 2 these patterns stay strings and every generated model that reaches the alias, directly or through other models, sets regex_engine="python-re", which works from Pydantic 2.5; hand-written models that embed generated ones must set it themselves, and an alias validated on its own then needs TypeAdapter(Alias, config=ConfigDict(regex_engine="python-re")). See Targeting a Pydantic version.

When --use-root-model-type-alias is enabled, roots with field constraints or patterns that require Python regex configuration use a regular RootModel class to preserve validation. Unconstrained roots and constraints already represented in the alias type keep the alias form. This does not change --use-type-alias. An existing custom pydantic_v2/RootModelTypeAlias.jinja2 remains selected; that template is responsible for preserving its root constraints.

items.title: API scope parameters
items.text:
Changed in 0.84.0

With --openapi-scopes api, OpenAPI path, query, header, and cookie parameter schemas that would be root models are always generated as type aliases, exactly as --use-type-alias emits them, whatever the output model type and options; 0.83.0 generated root models for them. Object parameters stay models, and component schemas keep their usual root models. See OpenAPI Options: Generate all API declarations.

items.title: API scope references
items.text:
Changed in 0.84.0

With --openapi-scopes api, a $ref beside only annotations such as description, title, examples, or x- extensions is the referenced model itself, so a parameter, body, or response that refers to a RootModel component is that RootModel rather than a second one wrapping it. Siblings that change the values, or nullable: true, still give a derived model. See OpenAPI Options: Generate all API declarations.

items.title: 📊 Type Alias Behavior by Output Type and Python Version
items.text:
The type of type alias generated depends on the output model type and target Python version:

Output Type Python 3.12+ Python 3.10-3.11 Pydantic v2 type statement TypeAliasType (typing_extensions) TypedDict type statement TypeAlias dataclasses type statement TypeAlias msgspec type statement TypeAlias

Use --use-type-alias-type to force TypeAliasType for TypedDict, dataclass, and msgspec output targeting Python 3.10 or 3.11. This option implies --use-type-alias, so the two flags do not need to be combined. Python 3.12 and newer still use the native type statement.

items.title: 🤔 Why the difference?
items.text:
• Pydantic v2 requires TypeAliasType because it cannot properly handle TypeAlias annotations
  • Other output types (TypedDict, dataclasses, msgspec) use TypeAlias for better compatibility with libraries that may not expect TypeAliasType objects
  • --use-type-alias-type opts into runtime TypeAliasType objects for those output types on Python 3.10-3.11
  • Python 3.12+ uses the native type statement for all output types

items.title: model.json
items.text:
{
  "$schema": "http://json-schema.org/draft-07/schema#",
  "definitions": {
    "UserId": {
      "type": "string"
    },
    "Status": {
      "anyOf": [
        {"type": "string"},
        {"type": "integer"}
      ]
    },
    "User": {
      "type": "object",
      "properties": {
        "id": {"$ref": "#/definitions/UserId"},
        "status": {"$ref": "#/definitions/Status"}
      }
    }
  }
}

items.title: Generating RootModel
items.text: datamodel-codegen --input model.json --input-file-type jsonschema --output-model-type pydantic_v2.BaseModel --output model.py

items.title: ✨ Generated model.py (Pydantic v2)
items.text:
# generated by datamodel-codegen:
#   filename:  model.json

from __future__ import annotations

from typing import Any, Optional, Union

from pydantic import BaseModel, RootModel


class Model(RootModel[Any]):
    root: Any


class UserId(RootModel[str]):
    root: str


class Status(RootModel[Union[str, int]]):
    root: Union[str, int]


class User(BaseModel):
    id: Optional[UserId] = None
    status: Optional[Status] = None

items.title: Generating type statement (Python 3.12+)
items.text: datamodel-codegen --input model.json --input-file-type jsonschema --output-model-type pydantic_v2.BaseModel --use-type-alias --target-python-version 3.12 --output model.py

items.title: ✨ Generated model.py (Python 3.12+ type statement)
items.text:
# generated by datamodel-codegen:
#   filename:  model.json

from __future__ import annotations

from typing import Any, Optional, Union

from pydantic import BaseModel

type Model = Any


type UserId = str


type Status = Union[str, int]


class User(BaseModel):
    id: Optional[UserId] = None
    status: Optional[Status] = None

items.title: 📚 Supported Input Formats
items.text:
This code generator supports the following input formats:

  • OpenAPI 3.0/3.1/3.2 (YAML/JSON, OpenAPI Data Types); OpenAPI 2.0 (Swagger) has limited support.
  • AsyncAPI 2.x/3.x (YAML/JSON).
  • JSON Schema (JSON Schema Core / JSON Schema Validation).
  • Apache Avro schema (.avsc, Apache Avro).
  • XML Schema (XSD).
  • Protocol Buffers / gRPC (.proto, Protocol Buffers / gRPC).
  • GraphQL schema (GraphQL Schemas and Types).
  • MCP tool schemas (--input-file-type mcp-tools, MCP Tool Schemas).
  • JSON / YAML / CSV data (converted to JSON Schema before model generation).
  • Python dictionary (converted to JSON Schema before model generation).
  • Existing Python types via --input-model: Pydantic models, dataclasses, Pydantic dataclasses, TypedDict, and dict schemas.

Use --input-file-type auto (the default) for common files, or set an explicit type when a file extension is ambiguous. For example, YAML can contain either an OpenAPI/JSON Schema document or raw sample data, so use jsonschema, openapi, or yaml depending on the intended input.

items.title: Schema Version Support
items.text: This document describes the JSON Schema, OpenAPI, AsyncAPI, Apache Avro, XML Schema, and Protocol Buffers versions supported by datamodel-code-generator.

items.title: Overview
items.text: datamodel-code-generator supports multiple schema formats including JSON Schema, OpenAPI, AsyncAPI, Apache Avro, XML Schema, and Protocol Buffers. By default, the tool operates in Lenient mode, accepting all features regardless of version declarations for formats that carry version information. This ensures maximum compatibility with real-world schemas that often mix features from different versions.

items.title: Version Detection
items.text:
datamodel-code-generator automatically detects the JSON Schema version:

  1. Explicit $schema field: If present, the version is detected from the URL pattern
  2. Heuristics: If no $schema, presence of $defs suggests 2020-12, definitions suggests Draft 7
  3. Fallback: Draft 7 (backward-compatible default)

items.title: Embedded Schema Resources
items.text: Nested $id declarations identify embedded schema resources. References to these resources resolve within the containing document before any file or HTTP lookup. Relative references inside each resource use its own URI as their base, and JSON pointers and anchors are scoped to that resource.

items.title: Version Detection
items.text:
datamodel-code-generator detects the OpenAPI version from the openapi field:

  • openapi: "3.0.x" -> OpenAPI 3.0
  • openapi: "3.1.x" -> OpenAPI 3.1
  • openapi: "3.2.x" -> OpenAPI 3.2
  • No openapi field -> Fallback to OpenAPI 3.1

items.title: MCP Tool Schema Profile Support
items.text:
MCP tool schema profile documents are supported with --input-file-type mcp-tools. This input type is experimental and converts MCP tool inputSchema and outputSchema entries into JSON Schema definitions before model generation.

Supported source shapes include:

  • tools/list JSON-RPC responses with result.tools;
  • MCP server definitions with a top-level tools array;
  • single tool definitions or arrays of tool definitions;
  • JSON Schema documents whose $defs or definitions values are tool definitions.

Each generated definition is named from the tool name plus Input or Output, for example SearchInput, SearchOutput, and CreateIssueInput.

items.text: Version Spec URL Notes proto2 protobuf.dev/reference/protobuf/proto2-spec required, optional, repeated, defaults, extensions proto3 protobuf.dev/reference/protobuf/proto3-spec implicit field defaults, optional, maps, services edition 2023 protobuf.dev/editions Supported by the bundled protoc runtime

items.title: Version Detection
items.text:
datamodel-code-generator detects Protocol Buffers syntax from each compiled .proto descriptor:

  • syntax = "proto3"; -> proto3
  • syntax = "proto2"; or no syntax declaration -> proto2
  • edition = "2023"; -> edition 2023
  • --schema-version proto2, --schema-version proto3, or --schema-version 2023 can override auto-detection

items.title: Apache Avro Schema Support
items.text: JSON-encoded Apache Avro schemas are supported with --input-file-type avro. The parser accepts .avsc files and Avro schema JSON.

items.title: Version Detection
items.text: Apache Avro schemas do not include an in-schema version marker equivalent to JSON Schema's $schema, OpenAPI's openapi, or XML Schema versioning attributes. For that reason, --schema-version does not select an Avro specification version. The Avro parser follows the currently implemented Apache Avro schema rules and logical types.

items.title: Avro Limitations
items.text: datamodel-code-generator generates Python model definitions from Avro schemas. It does not implement Avro runtime validation, binary encoding, decoding, or serialization.

items.title: Mixed Version Schemas
items.text:
Real-world schemas often mix features from different versions. datamodel-code-generator handles this in Lenient mode (default):

  • Features from all versions are accepted
  • No warnings for version mismatches
  • Maximum compatibility with existing schemas

In Strict mode (--schema-version-mode strict), warnings are emitted for version-incompatible features.

items.title: Type Mappings and Custom Types
items.text: datamodel-code-generator allows you to customize how schema types are mapped to Python types. This is essential for projects with specific type requirements, datetime handling preferences, or third-party library integrations.

items.title: Quick Overview
items.text: Option Description --type-mappings Map schema types to custom Python types --strict-types Use Pydantic strict types for validation --output-datetime-class Choose datetime output type --use-pendulum Use Pendulum library for datetime types --use-decimal-for-multiple-of Use Decimal for multipleOf constraints format: "email" Email validation (requires email-validator) format: "ulid" ULID type support (requires python-ulid)

items.title: --type-mappings
items.text: Maps schema type+format combinations to other format names. This allows you to override how specific formats are interpreted.

items.title: Format
items.text: --type-mappings <type+format>=<target_format> [<type+format>=<target_format> ...]

items.title: Basic Examples
items.text:
# Map binary format to string (generates str instead of bytes)
datamodel-codegen --input schema.json --output models.py \
  --type-mappings "binary=string"

# Map email format to string (generates str instead of EmailStr)
datamodel-codegen --input schema.json --output models.py \
  --type-mappings "string+email=string"

# Multiple mappings
datamodel-codegen --input schema.json --output models.py \
  --type-mappings "string+email=string" "string+uuid=string"

items.title: Mapping Syntax
items.text: Syntax Description Example format=target Map format (assumes string type) binary=string type+format=target Map type with format string+email=string

items.title: Avoiding Pydantic Optional Extras
items.text:
Some Pydantic types require optional dependencies. Use --type-mappings to generate plain types instead:

# Avoid pydantic[email] dependency (EmailStr requires email-validator)
--type-mappings "string+email=string" "string+idn-email=string"

# Generate str instead of UUID for uuid format
--type-mappings "string+uuid=string"

items.title: Available Target Formats
items.text: Target Generated Type string str integer int number float boolean bool binary bytes date datetime.date date-time datetime.datetime uuid UUID email EmailStr uri AnyUrl

items.title: pyproject.toml Configuration
items.text:
[tool.datamodel-codegen]
type-mappings = [
    "string+email=string",
    "string+idn-email=string",
    "binary=string",
]

items.title: --strict-types
items.text: Generates Pydantic strict types that don't perform type coercion during validation.

items.title: Available Strict Types
items.text:
Value Strict Type Rejects str StrictStr Integers, floats int StrictInt Strings, floats float StrictFloat Strings, integers bool StrictBool Strings, integers bytes StrictBytes Strings

A format: byte string stays Base64Str, or Base64Bytes with --type-mappings string+byte=binary, which decode base64 text, also with --strict-types str or bytes. With minLength or maxLength, such bytes are written as Annotated[bytes, Field(max_length=8), EncodedBytes(encoder=Base64Encoder)], which checks the lengths on the base64 text, as JSON Schema counts them, before decoding it. Pydantic checks them so from 2.10 on, and an explicit --target-pydantic-version 2 warns about each such field.

items.title: Without --strict-types
items.text:
class User(BaseModel):
    id: int  # Accepts "123" and converts to 123
    name: str  # Accepts 123 and converts to "123"
    active: bool  # Accepts 1 and converts to True

items.title: With --strict-types
items.text:
datamodel-codegen --input schema.json --output models.py \
  --strict-types str int bool

from pydantic import StrictBool, StrictInt, StrictStr


class User(BaseModel):
    id: StrictInt  # Rejects "123", requires integer
    name: StrictStr  # Rejects 123, requires string
    active: StrictBool  # Rejects 1, requires boolean

items.title: When to use
items.text:
• API validation where type coercion is undesirable
  • Data pipelines requiring exact types
  • Security-sensitive applications
  • Testing environments requiring strict type checking

items.title: --output-datetime-class
items.text:
Controls the Python type used for date-time formatted strings.

Value Output Type Description datetime datetime.datetime Standard library datetime (default) AwareDatetime pydantic.AwareDatetime Requires timezone info NaiveDatetime pydantic.NaiveDatetime Rejects timezone info

items.title: Default behavior
items.text:
from datetime import datetime


class Event(BaseModel):
    created_at: datetime  # Accepts both aware and naive

items.title: AwareDatetime (recommended for APIs)
items.text:
datamodel-codegen --input schema.json --output models.py \
  --output-datetime-class AwareDatetime

from pydantic import AwareDatetime


class Event(BaseModel):
    created_at: AwareDatetime  # Requires timezone, e.g., 2024-01-01T00:00:00Z

items.title: NaiveDatetime
items.text:
datamodel-codegen --input schema.json --output models.py \
  --output-datetime-class NaiveDatetime

from pydantic import NaiveDatetime


class Event(BaseModel):
    created_at: NaiveDatetime  # Rejects timezone, e.g., 2024-01-01T00:00:00

items.title: When to use each
items.text: Use Case Recommended Class REST APIs AwareDatetime Database models datetime or NaiveDatetime Logs with UTC timestamps AwareDatetime Local time applications NaiveDatetime

items.title: --use-pendulum
items.text:
Uses Pendulum library types instead of standard library datetime.

pip install pendulum
datamodel-codegen --input schema.json --output models.py --use-pendulum

items.title: Output
items.text:
import pendulum


class Event(BaseModel):
    created_at: pendulum.DateTime
    date: pendulum.Date
    time: pendulum.Time

items.title: Benefits of Pendulum
items.text:
• Timezone handling is simpler and more intuitive
  • Human-friendly datetime manipulation
  • Better serialization defaults
  • Immutable by default

items.title: When to use
items.text:
• Projects already using Pendulum
  • Applications requiring complex datetime manipulation
  • When timezone handling is a priority

items.title: Email Format Support
items.text:
The generator supports the email and idn-email string formats, which generate Pydantic's EmailStr type.

Required Dependency

The email format requires the email-validator package to be installed: 

pip install email-validator
Or install Pydantic with the email extra: 
pip install pydantic[email]

items.title: Schema Example
items.text:
{
  "type": "object",
  "properties": {
    "email": {
      "type": "string",
      "format": "email"
    }
  }
}

items.title: Output
items.text:
from pydantic import BaseModel, EmailStr


class MyModel(BaseModel):
    email: EmailStr

items.title: Avoiding the Dependency
items.text:
If you don't want to install email-validator, you can map email formats to plain strings:

datamodel-codegen --input schema.json --output models.py \
  --type-mappings "string+email=string" "string+idn-email=string"

This generates str instead of EmailStr.

items.title: ULID Format Support
items.text:
The generator supports the ulid string format, which generates python-ulid types.

Required Dependency

The ulid format requires the python-ulid package to be installed: 

pip install python-ulid
For Pydantic integration, use: 
pip install python-ulid[pydantic]

items.title: Schema Example
items.text:
{
  "type": "object",
  "properties": {
    "id": {
      "type": "string",
      "format": "ulid"
    }
  }
}

items.title: Output
items.text:
from ulid import ULID
from pydantic import BaseModel


class MyModel(BaseModel):
    id: ULID

items.title: What is ULID?
items.text:
ULID (Universally Unique Lexicographically Sortable Identifier) is an alternative to UUID that offers:

  • Lexicographic sorting - ULIDs sort naturally by creation time
  • Compactness - 26 characters vs 36 for UUID
  • URL-safe - Uses Crockford's Base32 encoding
  • Timestamp encoded - First 10 characters encode creation time

items.title: When to use
items.text:
• Distributed systems requiring time-ordered IDs
  • Applications where database index performance matters
  • When you need both uniqueness and sortability

items.title: --use-decimal-for-multiple-of
items.text: Uses Decimal type for numbers with multipleOf constraints to avoid floating-point precision issues.

items.title: The Problem
items.text:
properties:
  price:
    type: number
    multipleOf: 0.01  # Currency precision

Without this option, floating-point arithmetic can cause validation issues:

# 0.1 + 0.2 = 0.30000000000000004 in floating-point
price = 0.30000000000000004  # May fail multipleOf validation

items.title: Solution
items.text:
datamodel-codegen --input schema.json --output models.py \
  --use-decimal-for-multiple-of

from decimal import Decimal


class Product(BaseModel):
    price: Decimal  # Exact decimal arithmetic

items.title: When to use
items.text:
• Financial applications
  • Scientific calculations requiring precision
  • Any schema with multipleOf constraints

items.title: Forms and strict types
items.text: The default Pydantic output writes condecimal(...). With --field-constraints or --use-annotated the field is a Decimal with its constraints in Field(), for example Annotated[Decimal, Field(ge=0, multiple_of=0.01)]. Under --strict-types float the Decimal is strict: condecimal(..., strict=True), or strict=True among the Field() arguments. It rejects Python floats and, as Pydantic's strict Decimal does in JSON, accepts JSON numbers and numeric strings. A custom DataTypeManager receives every constraint of the schema in the field forms too, with field_constraints=True; the base class ignores them.

items.title: Pattern 1: Minimal dependencies
items.text:
Avoid optional Pydantic dependencies by mapping special formats to plain types:

datamodel-codegen --input schema.json --output models.py \
  --type-mappings "string+email=string" "string+idn-email=string"

items.title: Pattern 2: Strict API validation
items.text:
datamodel-codegen --input schema.json --output models.py \
  --strict-types str int float bool \
  --output-datetime-class AwareDatetime \
  --field-constraints

items.title: Pattern 3: Financial application
items.text:
datamodel-codegen --input schema.json --output models.py \
  --use-decimal-for-multiple-of \
  --strict-types str int

items.title: Pattern 4: Pendulum datetime handling
items.text:
datamodel-codegen --input schema.json --output models.py \
  --use-pendulum \
  --strict-types str int

items.title: Common Format Mappings
items.text:
Schema Format Default Type With --type-mappings "format=string" email EmailStr str idn-email EmailStr str uuid UUID str ulid ULID (requires python-ulid) str uri AnyUrl str binary bytes str

Other type customization options

For datetime types, use --output-datetime-class or --use-pendulum instead of --type-mappings.

items.title: 🐍 Using datamodel-code-generator as a Module
items.text: datamodel-code-generator is a CLI tool, but it can also be used as a Python module.

items.title: 🚀 How to Use
items.text: You can generate models with datamodel_code_generator.generate using parameters that match the CLI arguments.

items.title: 📦 Installation
items.text:
The base package is sufficient when all inputs and references are local. To load an HTTP(S) input or resolve a remote $ref, install the stable HTTP extra:

pip install 'datamodel-code-generator[http]'

The http extra uses HTTPX and is supported and not deprecated. The experimental HTTPX2 backend is available separately:

pip install 'datamodel-code-generator[httpx2]'

The experimental extra is not included in datamodel-code-generator[all]. The default HTTPBackend.AUTO policy selects stable HTTPX when its client module is installed, including when both extras are installed, and selects HTTPX2 only when that module is absent. Require HTTPX2 with --http-backend httpx2, http_backend = "httpx2" under [tool.datamodel-codegen], or the public API:

from urllib.parse import urlparse

from datamodel_code_generator import HTTPBackend, generate

result = generate(
    urlparse("https://example.com/schema.json"),
    http_backend=HTTPBackend.HTTPX2,
)

See HTTP backend selection for the complete automatic and explicit selection rules.

items.title: 📝 Getting Generated Code as String
items.text:
When the output parameter is omitted (or set to None), generate() returns the generated code directly as a string:

Note

GenerateConfig requires a Pydantic v2 environment.

from datamodel_code_generator import InputFileType, generate, GenerateConfig, DataModelType

json_schema: str = """{
    "type": "object",
    "properties": {
        "number": {"type": "number"},
        "street_name": {"type": "string"},
        "street_type": {"type": "string",
                        "enum": ["Street", "Avenue", "Boulevard"]
                        }
    }
}"""

config = GenerateConfig(
    input_file_type=InputFileType.JsonSchema,
    input_filename="example.json",
    output_model_type=DataModelType.PydanticV2BaseModel,
)
result = generate(json_schema, config=config)
print(result)

items.title: Loading Project Configuration
items.text:
generate() uses the options passed to it. The settings the command line implies apply the same way: msgspec.Struct output turns on use_annotated unless it is passed, and use_annotated turns on field_constraints. Pass use_annotated=False to keep msgspec models without Annotated constraints, as generate() wrote them before 0.84.0.

To reuse [tool.datamodel-codegen] from pyproject.toml, explicitly load a GenerateConfig:

from datamodel_code_generator import generate, load_pyproject_config

config = load_pyproject_config()
result = generate(json_schema, config=config)

The loader searches upward from the working directory, stopping at a Git project boundary, as the CLI does. Pass path="project", a Path, or a pyproject.toml path to start elsewhere, and profile="models" to select a profile, including its extends inheritance. Without project settings, it returns the API defaults; a requested profile must exist.

Both a GenerateConfig and a dictionary of individual Python API options can override the project settings:

from datamodel_code_generator import GenerateConfig, InputFileType

options = {"input_file_type": InputFileType.JsonSchema, "output": None}
config = load_pyproject_config(overrides=options)
result = generate(json_schema, config=config)

existing_config = GenerateConfig(output=None, disable_timestamp=True)
config = load_pyproject_config(profile="models", overrides=existing_config)
result = generate(json_schema, config=config)

The precedence is API defaults, project settings, profile settings, then overrides. Only explicitly set fields of a GenerateConfig override are merged; explicit False, None, and empty lists also replace project values. Paths loaded from TOML are relative to its directory, including JSON configuration files such as aliases, unlike the command line, which reads those JSON files from the working directory. Override paths remain relative to the caller's working directory. The project directory supplies formatter settings unless settings_path is explicitly overridden. CLI-only settings such as input, check, and batch jobs are ignored: pass the schema to generate() yourself. The loader validates the merged settings and preserves the existing rule that config= cannot be combined with individual generate() options.

items.title: 📝 Reading Input From a File
items.text:
Pass a Path to input_ for file input. Plain strings are treated as schema text; if a string points to an existing file and parsing fails, generate() warns and recommends using Path.

from pathlib import Path

from datamodel_code_generator import InputFileType, generate

result = generate(
    input_=Path("example.json"),
    input_file_type=InputFileType.JsonSchema,
)
print(result)

items.title: 📝 Multiple Module Output
items.text:
When the schema generates multiple modules, generate() returns a GeneratedModules dictionary mapping module path tuples to generated code:

from datamodel_code_generator import InputFileType, generate, GenerateConfig, GeneratedModules

# Your OpenAPI specification (string schema text, Path, or dict)
openapi_spec: str = "..."  # Replace with your actual OpenAPI spec

# Schema that generates multiple modules (e.g., with $ref to other files)
config = GenerateConfig(
    input_file_type=InputFileType.OpenAPI,
)
result: str | GeneratedModules = generate(openapi_spec, config=config)

if isinstance(result, dict):
    for module_path, content in result.items():
        print(f"Module: {'/'.join(module_path)}")
        print(content)
        print("---")
else:
    print(result)

items.title: 📝 Writing to Files
items.text:
To write generated code to the file system, provide a Path to the output parameter in the config:

from pathlib import Path
from tempfile import TemporaryDirectory
from datamodel_code_generator import InputFileType, generate, GenerateConfig, DataModelType

json_schema: str = """{
    "type": "object",
    "properties": {
        "number": {"type": "number"},
        "street_name": {"type": "string"},
        "street_type": {"type": "string",
                        "enum": ["Street", "Avenue", "Boulevard"]
                        }
    }
}"""

with TemporaryDirectory() as temporary_directory_name:
    temporary_directory = Path(temporary_directory_name)
    output = Path(temporary_directory / "model.py")
    config = GenerateConfig(
        input_file_type=InputFileType.JsonSchema,
        input_filename="example.json",
        output=output,
        # set up the output model types
        output_model_type=DataModelType.PydanticV2BaseModel,
    )
    generate(json_schema, config=config)
    model: str = output.read_text()
print(model)

✨ Output: 

# generated by datamodel-codegen:
#   filename:  example.json
#   timestamp: 2020-12-21T08:01:06+00:00

from __future__ import annotations

from enum import Enum
from typing import Optional

from pydantic import BaseModel


class StreetType(Enum):
    Street = "Street"
    Avenue = "Avenue"
    Boulevard = "Boulevard"


class Model(BaseModel):
    number: Optional[float] = None
    street_name: Optional[str] = None
    street_type: Optional[StreetType] = None

items.title: Generating a Server or Client Package
items.text:
Experimental

Server and client generation is experimental; its options and generated packages may change.

generate() also generates the FastAPI server or the HTTPX2 client package of an OpenAPI document together with its models. generate_server or generate_client selects the package, and the server_* or client_* options configure it. They are the options of --generate-server, --generate-client, and the --server-* and --client-* flags under their Python names, as for model options: choices are enums such as ServerType (their string values also work), and the options that take JSON on the command line take mappings.

from pathlib import Path

from datamodel_code_generator import (
    DataModelType,
    InputFileType,
    OpenAPIScope,
    ServerHandlerMode,
    ServerType,
    generate,
)

generate(
    Path("openapi.yaml"),
    input_file_type=InputFileType.OpenAPI,
    openapi_scopes=[OpenAPIScope.Schemas, OpenAPIScope.Api],
    output_model_type=DataModelType.PydanticV2BaseModel,
    preset="standard-py312-20261019",
    output=Path("app/models.py"),
    generate_server=ServerType.FastAPI,
    server_output=Path("app/server"),
    server_package="app.server",
    server_model_package="app.models",
    server_handler_mode=ServerHandlerMode.Async,
    server_body_modes={"/paths/~1upload/post": "request"},
)

With an output, generate() writes the models and the package together and returns None; for a server, it also writes each missing module of the services package beside the package once, with stubs, as the command line does. Without one, it writes nothing but the model metadata and a remote lock update, no stubs among them, and returns GeneratedModules with every model and package file, each under the path its import path implies: server_model_package="app.models" gives ("app", "models.py"), or ("app", "models", "__init__.py") and the other modules of modular models, and server_package="app.server" gives ("app", "server", "application.py"), ("app", "server", "README.md"), and so on. These are the files a run with output and server_output in the working directory writes; server_output is not used. The run renders the files in a private directory of the working directory, which it removes afterwards, so the working directory must be writable. load_pyproject_config() takes the server and client keys of pyproject.toml too, so a config it loads with overrides={"output": None} returns the files of the configured run.

The selector requires server_package and server_model_package (or the client ones), and server_output with an output. A model setting the target needs that neither the arguments nor the preset set, such as openapi_scopes or target_python_version, takes the value the target needs, without printing anything; see Requirements. A missing option, an option the target cannot use, and a failure of the package raise datamodel_code_generator.Error with the message the command line prints. The server_* and client_* options have no effect without their selector, as their pyproject.toml keys do.

items.title: 🔧 Using the Parser Directly
items.text: You can also call the parser directly for more control. Parser classes also support the config parameter similar to generate().

items.title: Using config Parameter (Recommended)
items.text:
from datamodel_code_generator import DataModelType, PythonVersion
from datamodel_code_generator.config import JSONSchemaParserConfig
from datamodel_code_generator.model import get_data_model_types
from datamodel_code_generator.parser.jsonschema import JsonSchemaParser

json_schema: str = """{
    "type": "object",
    "properties": {
        "number": {"type": "number"},
        "street_name": {"type": "string"},
        "street_type": {"type": "string",
                        "enum": ["Street", "Avenue", "Boulevard"]
                        }
    }
}"""

data_model_types = get_data_model_types(DataModelType.PydanticV2BaseModel, target_python_version=PythonVersion.PY_311)
config = JSONSchemaParserConfig(
    data_model_type=data_model_types.data_model,
    data_model_root_type=data_model_types.root_model,
    data_model_field_type=data_model_types.field_model,
    data_type_manager_type=data_model_types.data_type_manager,
    dump_resolve_reference_action=data_model_types.dump_resolve_reference_action,
)
parser = JsonSchemaParser(json_schema, config=config)
result = parser.parse()
print(result)

items.title: Field Validators
items.text: The --validators option allows you to add custom field validators to generated Pydantic v2 models. This enables you to inject validation logic into generated code without manually editing it.

items.title: Basic Usage
items.text:
datamodel-codegen --input schema.json --output model.py \
  --validators validators.json \
  --use-annotated \
  --output-model-type pydantic_v2.BaseModel

You can also pass the same JSON object inline:

datamodel-codegen --input schema.json --output model.py \
  --validators '{"User":{"validators":[{"field":"name","function":"myapp.validators.validate_name"}]}}' \
  --use-annotated \
  --output-model-type pydantic_v2.BaseModel

items.title: Validators Format
items.text: The validators JSON maps model names to their validator definitions. Pass it either inline or as a JSON file path.

items.title: Structure
items.text:
{
  "ModelName": {
    "validators": [
      {
        "field": "field_name",
        "function": "module.path.to.validator_function",
        "mode": "after"
      }
    ]
  }
}

items.title: Fields
items.text: Field Description Required field Single field name to validate One of field or fields fields List of field names (for multi-field validators) One of field or fields function Fully qualified path to the validator function Yes mode Validator mode: before, after, wrap, or plain No (default: after)

items.title: Validator Modes
items.text: Pydantic v2 supports different validator modes, each with its own signature:

items.title: before / after Mode
items.text:
Standard validators that run before or after Pydantic's own validation:

def validate_name(v: Any, info: ValidationInfo) -> Any:
    if not v:
        raise ValueError("Name cannot be empty")
    return v.strip()

items.title: wrap Mode
items.text:
Wrap validators receive a handler to call the next validator in the chain:

from pydantic import ValidationInfo, ValidatorFunctionWrapHandler


def wrap_validate_name(v: Any, handler: ValidatorFunctionWrapHandler, info: ValidationInfo) -> Any:
    # Pre-processing
    v = v.strip() if isinstance(v, str) else v
    # Call next validator
    result = handler(v)
    # Post-processing
    return result.upper()

items.title: plain Mode
items.text:
Plain validators replace Pydantic's validation entirely:

def plain_validate_name(v: Any) -> str:
    if not isinstance(v, str):
        raise TypeError("Expected string")
    return v

items.title: Input Schema
items.text:
{
  "type": "object",
  "title": "User",
  "properties": {
    "name": {"type": "string"},
    "email": {"type": "string", "format": "email"},
    "age": {"type": "integer", "minimum": 0}
  },
  "required": ["name", "email"]
}

items.title: Validators File
items.text:
{
  "User": {
    "validators": [
      {
        "field": "name",
        "function": "myapp.validators.validate_name",
        "mode": "before"
      },
      {
        "field": "email",
        "function": "myapp.validators.validate_email",
        "mode": "after"
      },
      {
        "fields": ["name", "email"],
        "function": "myapp.validators.validate_contact_info",
        "mode": "after"
      }
    ]
  }
}

items.title: Validator Functions (myapp/validators.py)
items.text:
from typing import Any
from pydantic import ValidationInfo


def validate_name(v: Any, info: ValidationInfo) -> Any:
    if isinstance(v, str):
        return v.strip()
    return v


def validate_email(v: Any, info: ValidationInfo) -> Any:
    if isinstance(v, str) and not v.endswith("@example.com"):
        # Custom email domain validation
        pass
    return v


def validate_contact_info(v: Any, info: ValidationInfo) -> Any:
    # This runs for both name and email fields
    return v

items.title: Generated Output
items.text:
from __future__ import annotations

from typing import Annotated, Any

from myapp.validators import validate_contact_info, validate_email, validate_name
from pydantic import BaseModel, EmailStr, Field, ValidationInfo, field_validator


class User(BaseModel):
    name: str
    email: EmailStr
    age: Annotated[int | None, Field(ge=0)] = None

    @field_validator("name", mode="before")
    @classmethod
    def validate_name_validator(cls, v: Any, info: ValidationInfo) -> Any:
        return validate_name(v, info)

    @field_validator("email", mode="after")
    @classmethod
    def validate_email_validator(cls, v: Any, info: ValidationInfo) -> Any:
        return validate_email(v, info)

    @field_validator("name", "email", mode="after")
    @classmethod
    def validate_contact_info_validator(cls, v: Any, info: ValidationInfo) -> Any:
        return validate_contact_info(v, info)

items.title: Notes
items.text:
• This feature only supports Pydantic v2 (--output-model-type pydantic_v2.BaseModel)
  • The ModelName in the validators JSON must match the generated Python class name
  • Validator functions are imported automatically based on the function path
  • When validator method names collide with another validator, an existing field, or an inherited validator, an incrementing suffix (_1, _2, etc.) is added in registration order.
  • Functions with the same name from different modules receive stable import aliases using the same suffix format. Repeated uses of the same function share its import binding; every validator registration is retained.

items.title: 🧾 Generate from XML Schema
items.text:
Generate Python models from W3C XML Schema documents (.xsd).

Experimental

XML Schema input support is experimental and may change as real-world usage is validated.

items.title: 🚀 Quick Start
items.text:
datamodel-codegen \
    --input purchase_order.xsd \
    --input-file-type xmlschema \
    --output-model-type pydantic_v2.BaseModel \
    --output model.py

items.title: 📝 Example
items.text:
purchase_order.xsd 

<xs:schema xmlns:xs="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema">
  <xs:element name="purchaseOrder" type="PurchaseOrder"/>

  <xs:complexType name="PurchaseOrder">
    <xs:sequence>
      <xs:element name="id" type="xs:string"/>
      <xs:element name="total" type="xs:decimal"/>
    </xs:sequence>
  </xs:complexType>
</xs:schema>

✨ Generated model.py 

from __future__ import annotations

from decimal import Decimal

from pydantic import BaseModel


class PurchaseOrder(BaseModel):
    id: str
    total: Decimal

items.title: Supported XML Schema Versions
items.text: The XML Schema parser supports XML Schema 1.0 and selected XML Schema 1.1 constructs. Use --schema-version auto to detect the version from versioning attributes and XSD 1.1 constructs, or pass --schema-version 1.0 / --schema-version 1.1 explicitly.

items.title: Supported XML Schema Features
items.text:
The XML Schema parser converts XSD into the JSON Schema shape used by the normal model-generation pipeline. It supports the constructs needed to generate Python model definitions:

XSD construct Model generation behavior Built-in simple types Maps XML Schema scalar types to Python scalar types xs:complexType Generates a Python model class xs:simpleType restrictions Generates constrained scalar fields where possible xs:sequence, xs:choice, xs:all Generates fields from model particles minOccurs, maxOccurs, nillable Preserves optionality, lists, and nullability Attributes Generates model fields for XML attributes xs:include, xs:import, xs:redefine, xs:override Resolves local schema composition Namespaces Uses namespace context to avoid name collisions Substitution groups and wildcards Generates compatible model shapes where possible

items.title: Limitations
items.text:
The XML Schema input type is for generating Python model definitions. It does not implement XML parsing, XML serialization, or runtime XML validation.

Generated Pydantic v2 pattern constraints that combine distinct facets in the same restriction, or inherited and derived facets, require Pydantic 2.8 or later in the environment that runs the generated code, for every --target-pydantic-version including 2. These constraints use compiled Python regular expressions to preserve full-value matching and inherited restrictions, including when a generated type alias is used directly with TypeAdapter. Pydantic 2.8 added support for compiled patterns. This does not add generated validators or change the Pydantic requirement for other XSD inputs or input formats. Upgrading only the environment that runs datamodel-code-generator does not upgrade the generated code's runtime.

Python properties use XML local names. Generation fails when distinct XML names would overwrite the same property, such as an element and attribute named code, or elements named code in different namespaces. Repeated uses of the same XML name remain supported.

items.title: --emit-model-metadata
items.text:
Write a separate JSON map from the final generated models, modules, fields, and type hints to the JSON Pointer locations of their source schemas. Several models can share one location, such as read and write variants of one schema, so the module and class name identify a model.

Usage

datamodel-codegen --input model_metadata.json --emit-model-metadata model-map.json --module-split-mode single --disable-timestamp # (1)!
  1. --emit-model-metadata - the option documented here
Examples

Input Schema:

{
  "$schema": "https://json-schema.org/draft/2020-12/schema",
  "title": "Root title",
  "type": "object",
  "properties": {
    "method": {
      "const": "thread/started"
    },
    "payload": {
      "$ref": "#/$defs/MetadataPayload"
    }
  },
  "required": ["method", "payload"],
  "$defs": {
    "MetadataPayload": {
      "title": "Payload title",
      "type": "object",
      "properties": {
        "id": {
          "type": "integer"
        }
      },
      "required": ["id"]
    }
  }
}

items.title: --encoding
items.text:
Specify character encoding for input and output files.

The --encoding flag sets the character encoding used when reading the schema file and writing the generated Python code. This is useful for schemas containing non-ASCII characters (e.g., Japanese, Chinese). Default is UTF-8, which is the standard encoding for JSON and most modern text files.

Usage

datamodel-codegen --input encoding_test.json --encoding utf-8 # (1)!
  1. --encoding - the option documented here
Examples

Input Schema:

{
  "$schema": "http://json-schema.org/draft-07/schema#",
  "title": "日本語Model",
  "description": "モデルの説明文",
  "type": "object",
  "properties": {
    "名前": {
      "type": "string",
      "description": "ユーザー名"
    },
    "年齢": {
      "type": "integer"
    }
  }
}

from pydantic import BaseModel, Field


class 日本語Model(BaseModel):
    名前: str | None = Field(None, description='ユーザー名')
    年齢: int | None = None

items.title: --external-ref-mapping
items.text:
Map external $ref files to Python packages.

Use --external-ref-mapping FILE_PATH=PYTHON_PACKAGE to import referenced models from an existing package, instead of generating duplicate classes from external schema files.

Usage

datamodel-codegen --input api.yaml --input-file-type openapi --external-ref-mapping common.yaml=mypackage.shared.models # (1)!
  1. --external-ref-mapping - the option documented here
Examples

Input Schema:

info:
  title: API
  version: "1.0.0"
paths: {}
components:
  schemas:
    UserResponse:
      type: object
      properties:
        user:
          $ref: "common.yaml#/components/schemas/User"
        request_id:
          type: string
      required:
        - user
        - request_id
    ErrorResponse:
      type: object
      properties:
        error:
          $ref: "common.yaml#/components/schemas/Error"
        timestamp:
          type: string
          format: date-time
      required:
        - error
        - timestamp

items.title: --input-file-type
items.text:
Specify the input file type for code generation.

The --input-file-type flag explicitly sets the input format.

Important distinction:

  • Use jsonschema, openapi, asyncapi, graphql, mcp-tools, xmlschema, protobuf, or avro for schema definition files
  • Use json, yaml, or csv for raw sample data to automatically infer a schema

For example, if you have a JSON Schema written in YAML format, use --input-file-type jsonschema, not --input-file-type yaml. The yaml type treats the file as raw data and infers a schema from it.

Usage

datamodel-codegen --input pet.json --input-file-type json # (1)!
  1. --input-file-type - the option documented here
Examples JSONYAML

Input Schema:

{
  "Pet": {
    "name": "dog",
    "age": 2
  }
}

Output:

# generated by datamodel-codegen:
#   filename:  pet.json
#   timestamp: 2019-07-26T00:00:00+00:00

from __future__ import annotations

from pydantic import BaseModel, Field


class Pet(BaseModel):
    name: str
    age: int


class Model(BaseModel):
    Pet_1: Pet = Field(..., alias='Pet')

Pet:
  name: cat
  age: 3

    age: int

items.title: --input-model-ref-strategy

Strategy for referenced types when using --input-model.

The --input-model-ref-strategy option determines whether to regenerate or import referenced types. Use regenerate-all (default) to regenerate all types, reuse-foreign to import types from different families (like enums when generating dataclasses) while regenerating same-family types, or reuse-all to import all referenced types directly.

Usage

items.title: --preset
items.text:
Apply an immutable built-in option preset.

The standard-py312-20260619 preset enables the recommended modern Python output style for new projects. The preset name pins generated Python syntax and backports.

Related: --target-python-version

See also: pyproject.toml Configuration

Usage

datamodel-codegen --input person.json --preset standard-py312-20260619 # (1)!

Input Schema:

{
  "$schema": "http://json-schema.org/draft-07/schema#",
  "title": "Person",
  "type": "object",
  "properties": {
    "firstName": {
      "type": "string",
      "description": "The person's first name."
    },
    "lastName": {
      "type": ["string", "null"],
      "description": "The person's last name."
    },
    "age": {
      "description": "Age in years which must be equal to or greater than zero.",
      "type": "integer",
      "minimum": 0

    },
    "comment": {
      "type": "null"
    }
  }
}

from typing import Annotated, Any

from pydantic import BaseModel, ConfigDict, Field


class Person(BaseModel):
    model_config = ConfigDict(
        populate_by_name=True,
    )
    first_name: Annotated[
        str | None, Field(alias='firstName', description="The person's first name.")
    ] = None
    last_name: Annotated[
        str | None, Field(alias='lastName', description="The person's last name.")
    ] = None
    age: Annotated[
        int | None,
        Field(
            description='Age in years which must be equal to or greater than zero.',
            ge=0,
        ),
    ] = None
    friends: list[Any] | None = None

items.title: --schema-version
items.text:
Schema version to use for parsing.

The --schema-version option specifies the schema version to use instead of auto-detection. Valid values depend on input type: JsonSchema (draft-04, draft-06, draft-07, 2019-09, 2020-12) or OpenAPI (3.0, 3.1, 3.2). Default is 'auto' (detected from $schema or openapi field).

Usage

datamodel-codegen --input simple_string.json --schema-version draft-07 # (1)!
  1. --schema-version - the option documented here
Examples OpenAPIJSON Schema

Input Schema:

openapi: "3.0.0"
info:
  version: 1.0.0
  title: Swagger Petstore
  license:
    name: MIT
servers:
  - url: http://petstore.swagger.io/v1

  /pets:
    get:
      summary: List all pets
      operationId: listPets
      tags:
        - pets
      parameters:
        - name: limit

          required: false
          schema:
            type: integer
            format: int32
      responses:
        '200':
          description: A paged array of pets
          headers:
            x-next:
              description: A link to the next page of responses
              schema:
                type: string
          content:

              schema:
                $ref: "#/components/schemas/Pets"
        default:
          description: unexpected error

                x-amazon-apigateway-integration:

                    Fn::Sub: arn:aws:apigateway:${AWS::Region}:lambda:path/2015-03-31/functions/${PythonVersionFunction.Arn}/invocations
                  passthroughBehavior: when_no_templates
                  httpMethod: POST
                  type: aws_proxy
    post:
      summary: Create a pet
      operationId: createPets
      tags:
        - pets
      responses:
        '201':

                  passthroughBehavior: when_no_templates
                  httpMethod: POST

        default:

    x-amazon-apigateway-integration:
      uri:

      type: aws_proxy

items.title: --deserialize-default-values
items.text:
Deserialize selected direct scalar field defaults into their generated Python types.

The --deserialize-default-values option accepts an explicit list of generated value types. For example, --deserialize-default-values decimal emits a direct Decimal field's valid string default as a Decimal value, while --deserialize-default-values enum emits matching scalar and list defaults as enum members. items.title: --infer-union-variant-names
items.text:
Name inline oneOf/anyOf branch models after the value of their tag field (Pet + type: "cat" -> PetCat) instead of Pet1, Pet2.

The --infer-union-variant-names flag uses branch-local const values or single-value enums on a shared discriminator-style property to name generated inline union models. This is useful when inline union branches would otherwise receive position-based names such as Event and Event1.

The literal value can also come from a single-value enum or an internal $ref. At least two branches need distinct values on the field; to also name a union's only tagged branch and branches tagged by their only key, use --use-tag-as-union-variant-name. Do not write a constraint again beside a type that already enforces it.

In the field forms (--field-constraints, --use-annotated), a zero-bound class from --use-non-positive-negative-number-constrained-types, such as NonNegativeInt, enforces its bound, so a nullable field, a root model or an item writes NonNegativeInt | None instead of repeating Field(ge=0); under --strict-types the field writes the bound beside StrictInt instead of a strict conint. The Literal of a const or an enum enforces the length and number constraints beside it by its values: values that violate them are left out and the field writes none of them, and a const branch of a oneOf or anyOf whose constraints its value meets stays a Literal instead of a root model. A pattern and a multipleOf the check cannot decide stay written.

items.title: --use-site-models-for-constrained-refs
items.text:
Give an allOf of $ref members whose other parts add assertions its own model.

Without the option such an allOf is written as the referenced type, which leaves out the constraints, the enum values or the type its other parts add: allOf: [{$ref: Quantity}], maximum: 10 accepts 11. With the option the site gets its own model of the values all parts admit (conint(ge=1, le=10)), named after the site, and an allOf of enum references gets an enum of the members they share. The referenced type stays where it enforces what the parts enforce together in the output (dataclasses and TypedDict check no constraints, so only types and literals count there), and msgspec writes the added constraints beside the reference where its Meta takes them. A model-level --type-overrides entry of the referenced model applies to its site models too.

Usage

datamodel-codegen --input site_models_for_constrained_refs.json --use-site-models-for-constrained-refs # (1)!
  1. --use-site-models-for-constrained-refs - the option documented here
Examples

          "$ref": "#/$defs/Quantity"
        }
      ],
      "maximum": 10
    },
    "sizes": {
      "type": "array",
      "items": {
        "allOf": [
          {
            "$ref": "#/$defs/Size"
          },
          {
            "enum": [
              "m",
              "l"
            ]
          }
        ]
      }
    }
  },
  "$defs": {
    "Quantity": {
      "type": "integer",
      "minimum": 1
    },
    "Size": {

        "s",

      ]

items.title: --use-tag-as-union-variant-name
items.text:
Name inline oneOf/anyOf branch models after their tag: what --infer-union-variant-names does, skipping tags whose class names collide, plus single-branch unions (type: "exec" -> LocalShellActionExec) and single-key branches ({"granular": ...} -> AskForApprovalGranular).

--infer-union-variant-names needs at least two branches with distinct literals on one field, so a union with one tagged branch keeps a position-based name that changes once a second branch is added, and a branch tagged by its only key, as in externally tagged enums, is never named. --use-tag-as-union-variant-name gives the names --infer-union-variant-names gives wherever that option names a union with distinct class names, and in the other unions also names:

  • the branches after a literal field that only one branch carries or that the key branches below lack, picked like --infer-union-variant-names picks it (the discriminator property first, then property order) except that a field the union schema itself fixes to a single literal is skipped; a branch that is a union itself is not named this way;
  • a key branch after its key: its only own property (one the union schema does not declare), required and not a single literal, when the branch has no oneOf/anyOf and no allOf of its own that adds properties (the union schema's allOf is shared by every branch), and fixes no field the union declares without a literal to a single literal, unless the union is one branch beside null.

String enum branches and branches with several untagged properties keep position-based names. Names are compared as the class names they become, so foo-bar and fooBar (both FooBar) collide: a literal field whose names collide is skipped for the next one, and literal names win over key names, so a key name that collides with a literal name or another key name is dropped and its branch keeps a position-based name.

Under --naming-strategy parent-prefixed or full-path, a model in the value of a branch named after its key is named as if the branch were not in its path, so the key is not repeated: the branch ItemEditedChangesFieldValue holds ItemEditedFieldValue, not ItemEditedChangesFieldValueFieldValue, numbered like any other name when another model has it.

Branches default --infer-union-variant-names --use-tag-as-union-variant-name Several branches, distinct type literals Pet1, Pet2 PetCat, PetDog PetCat, PetDog Single branch (type: "exec") LocalShellAction1 LocalShellAction1 LocalShellActionExec Single-key branch ({"granular": ...}) AskForApproval2 AskForApproval2 AskForApprovalGranular

items.title: --all-exports-collision-strategy
items.text:
Handle name collisions when exporting recursive module hierarchies.

The --all-exports-collision-strategy flag determines how to resolve naming conflicts when using --all-exports-scope=recursive. The 'minimal-prefix' strategy adds the minimum module path prefix needed to disambiguate colliding names, while 'full-prefix' uses the complete module path. Requires --all-exports-scope=recursive.

Related: --all-exports-scope

items.title: --allow-private-network
items.text:
Allow HTTP requests to private network schema endpoints.

The --allow-private-network flag permits trusted HTTP(S) schema requests to private, loopback, link-local, or otherwise non-public network hosts. Without this flag, those targets are blocked by default to reduce server-side request forgery (SSRF) risk. If a trusted internal schema endpoint is blocked, verify the URL and pass --allow-private-network; otherwise use a local schema file or public endpoint.

Usage

datamodel-codegen --url http://127.0.0.1/schema.json --allow-private-network # (1)!

items.title: --diff-against
items.text:
Compare generated code from a baseline input with the current schema without writing files.

Pass the baseline input with --diff-against and the current schema with --input. The command generates both, then shows the generated-code diff from baseline to current. The required --output value is a virtual destination: it selects single-file or directory layout and formatter settings, but datamodel-code-generator never writes it. The command exits non-zero when the formatted generated outputs differ, making it useful for reviewing schema migrations in CI.

Related: --check, --input, --output, --output-format

Option relationships:

  • Requires: --input - --diff-against requires --input with the current local schema path.
  • Requires: --output - --diff-against requires --output to select file or directory output layout.
  • Conflicts: --check
  • Conflicts: --watch
  • Conflicts: --url
  • Conflicts: --input-model
  • Conflicts: --emit-model-metadata
  • Conflicts: --fail-on-multi-module-stdout
  • Conflicts: --job - --diff-against compares one profile or input and cannot run named jobs.
  • Conflicts: --all-jobs - --diff-against compares one profile or input and cannot run named jobs.

Usage

datamodel-codegen --input tests/data/openapi/input_diff/new.yaml --diff-against tests/data/openapi/input_diff/old.yaml --output models --input-file-type openapi --disable-timestamp # (1)!
  1. --diff-against - the option documented here
Examples

Input Schema:

openapi: 3.0.0
info:
  title: Current models
  version: "1.0"
paths: {}
components:
  schemas:
    collections.Current:
      type: object
      properties:
        name:
          type: string

REMOVED: models.py (generated only from baseline input)

items.title: --fail-on-multi-module-stdout
items.text:
Fail instead of concatenating multiple modules in text stdout.

The --fail-on-multi-module-stdout flag detects modular results while preserving the legacy default, single-module output, JSON output, and file output. It takes precedence over automatic unusable-stdout repair, rejecting the modular result instead of coalescing it.

items.title: --http-local-ref-path
items.text:
Resolve HTTP references from local schema files.

The --http-local-ref-path flag maps HTTP(S) $ref URLs to files under a local schema store instead of fetching them from the network. items.title: --locked
items.text:
Require an existing remote lock and validate each fetched resource against it (experimental).

--locked fails if the selected lock is missing, a resource is unrecorded, or its body differs. It conflicts with --update-lock.

Remote reference lock support is experimental: its lock document schema and request-identity compatibility may evolve. It remains fail-closed on integrity mismatches, and it never persists credentials.

The lock stores opaque SHA-256 request-identity digests and SHA-256 body digests, never response bodies or request values directly. Each saved display origin contains only the scheme, host, and explicit port—never a path, query, or request headers. A request identity includes its scheme, host, explicit port, path, header names, and ordered query parameter names only. If one generation receives different bodies for the same path and query-name identity, it fails closed rather than sharing a lock entry.

Related: --http-local-ref-path, --lockfile, --url

Option relationships:

  • Conflicts: --update-lock

Usage

datamodel-codegen --url https://api.example.com/schema.json --locked --lockfile datamodel-codegen.lock # (1)!

items.title: --lockfile
items.text:
Select the remote reference integrity lock file (experimental).

An existing selected lock is verified automatically; a missing selected lock is ignored unless --locked requires it. Without --lockfile, the CLI uses datamodel-codegen.lock beside the discovered pyproject.toml, or in the invocation working directory when no project is found. Explicit relative --lockfile paths resolve from the invocation working directory, not the project root or output directory. The public API uses the caller's working directory for both its default lock and relative lockfile paths.

Remote reference lock support is experimental: its lock document schema and request-identity compatibility may evolve. It remains fail-closed on integrity mismatches, and it never persists credentials.

The lock stores opaque SHA-256 request-identity digests and SHA-256 body digests, never response bodies or request values directly. Each saved display origin contains only the scheme, host, and explicit port—never a path, query, or request headers. A request identity includes its scheme, host, explicit port, path, header names, and ordered query parameter names only. If one generation receives different bodies for the same path and query-name identity, it fails closed rather than sharing a lock entry.

items.title: --recommend-options
items.text:
Recommend options for the input schema on top of the latest dated preset (experimental).

--recommend-options reads the input schema, measures how it is written (shared property names, inline enums and objects, repeated shapes, titles, tagged unions, dotted keys, constraint keywords and formats), and applies the recommender's rule data. For a schema of up to 3000 estimated models, it then generates the candidate configurations in memory (the preset, the recommendation, and the recommendation without or with each option), compares their class names and the fields generated without their constraints, and recommends the best candidate, with class names before and after each option. It prints the latest dated preset to start from, the options to add with the reason for each, optional validation and policy options that stay out of the command, options it advises against, the compared candidates, and the resulting command and pyproject.toml block. Nothing is written. Options set on the command line or in pyproject.toml are kept and reported when the rules suggest another value. Add --output-format json for a structured payload, or --generate-prompt to include the recommendation in an LLM prompt instead.

Related: --enum-field-as-literal, --generate-prompt, --naming-strategy, --output-format, --preset

Usage

datamodel-codegen --input api.yaml --input-file-type openapi --recommend-options # (1)!
